title: The Sub-Creator's Road: Bloemfontein to Wolvercote
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Veldt and the Exile, Bloemfontein to Birmingham

stops.name: Bloemfontein, the birthplace on the high veldt
stops.campa: On the third of January, in the parched capital of the Orange Free State, John Ronald Reuel Tolkien is born to Arthur, an English bank manager, and Mabel his wife. The land is bare and hot, a wide emptiness of dust and enormous sky; the child's first world is the blank horizon and the stars strewn thick above it. Into the bank-house garden a great hairy spider comes and bites the toddling boy; his nurse sucks out the venom. The wound heals, the memory sinks, but the dry plains and the crawling terror both go down into the deep well from which Rohan and Shelob will one day rise.
suggested_refs: photograph of Arthur and Mabel Tolkien

stops.name: The Cathedral church, Bloemfontein: christened John Ronald Reuel
stops.campa: On the last day of January the infant is carried to the Anglican cathedral of the frontier town and christened John Ronald Reuel: Reuel a family name he never fully explains, which he will hand on to his own son. Arthur, prospering at the bank, means to raise his boys in Africa. But the harsh climate wastes the elder child, and within three years Mabel sails home to Birmingham for their health, leaving Arthur to follow. He never does: in February 1896 rheumatic fever and a brain haemorrhage take him, and he is buried at Bloemfontein, an ocean from his sons. The boy is fatherless at four.
suggested_refs: Cathedral of St Andrew and St Michael, Bloemfontein
grave of Arthur Reuel Tolkien, Bloemfontein

stops.name: Sarehole Mill, the green heart of the Shire
stops.campa: Mabel brings her two boys home to England, and after Arthur dies in Africa she settles them at Sarehole, a Worcestershire hamlet beneath a great water-mill. Here the exile of the veldt is answered: a lost paradise of meadow, millpond and the wooded bog. The boy roams with his brother Hilary, dreads the white-dusted miller's son they call the White Ogre, filches mushrooms from the farmer's field. Mabel teaches them at home: Latin, botany, the look and feel of trees. This bright, small English country, held only four years, becomes forever the model of the Shire, the homeland worth defending.
stops.quote: I could draw you a map of every inch of it. I loved it with an (idealised) love.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on Sarehole, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: The Birmingham Oratory and Rednal, the mother's death
stops.campa: Mabel, received into the Roman Church in 1900, is cut off by her Baptist kin for it, and sinks into poverty and illness. In the summer she lodges the boys in a cottage at Rednal by the Oratory's country house. There, on the fourteenth of November, in a diabetic coma, she dies at thirty-four. Ronald is twelve. He holds her ever after as a martyr who gave her life for the faith she would not renounce, and from her death he draws a lifelong grief-bright Catholicism, and the conviction woven through all his work that the world is fallen, its truest note the long defeat lit by sudden joy.
stops.quote: My own dear mother was a martyr indeed, and it is not to everybody that God grants so easy a way to his great gifts as he did to Hilary and myself, giving us a mother who killed herself with labour and trouble to ensure us keeping the faith.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 267 (to Michael Tolkien)

segments.name: The Two Towers of Boyhood: King Edward's, Edith, the T.C.B.S.

stops.name: King Edward's School, Birmingham: the philologist forged
stops.campa: On a Foundation Scholarship the orphan enters the great grammar school under the shadow of the two towers of the Oratory. Here his gift declares itself: Latin and Greek, then Anglo-Saxon, Gothic, Middle English, the Welsh names glimpsed on Welsh coal-trucks that he finds heart-piercingly beautiful. He begins, in boyhood, to invent tongues: first playful nonsense, then true grammars with sound-laws and histories. He is caught not by the meaning of words but by their music; 'cellar door', he will say, is a beautiful sound. Language is not his tool but his desire; the mythology, he confesses, is made to give his languages a world to be spoken in.
stops.quote: The invention of languages is the foundation. The 'stories' were made rather to provide a world for the languages than the reverse.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 165
suggested_refs: Perrott's Folly and the Oratory towers

stops.name: The railway sidings, the Welsh names on the coal-trucks
stops.campa: Along the Birmingham lines the coal-trucks come up from the valleys of South Wales bearing painted names: Nantyglo, Senghenydd, Blaen-Rhondda, Penrhiwceiber. And the boy reads them from the embankment as a kind of enchantment. He cannot understand a word, yet the shapes and sounds pierce him with a longing he cannot name, a beauty in the very grain of the language. This first wound of Welsh never closes; decades on it flowers into Sindarin, the Grey-elven tongue, patterned on the music of Welsh. His languages are born of desire before they are ever built of grammar.
stops.quote: The fluidity of Welsh, with peculiar phonetic charm . . . its 'wildness and beauty' appeals to me.
stops.quote_source: 'English and Welsh' (1955); Letters, no. 165

stops.name: 37 Duchess Road, Edith Bratt across the landing
stops.campa: Father Francis Morgan, guardian of the orphaned brothers, lodges them in a boarding-house where a fellow lodger is Edith Bratt, herself an orphan, three years older, a fine pianist. The two conspire: they haunt Birmingham teashops, sit on a balcony above the street, and drop sugar-lumps into the hats of passers-by. By the summer of 1909 they are in love. It is a first, secret, whole-hearted love, and it will echo down the years into a tale of a mortal man and an immortal maid who dances in a wood, the greatest of the stories of the Elder Days.
suggested_refs: photograph of Edith Bratt as a young woman

stops.name: Barrow's Stores, the Tea Club and Barrovian Society
stops.campa: In the school library and in the tea-room of Barrow's Stores four boys form a secret fellowship, brewing clandestine tea and reading their poems and enthusiasms aloud. They are Tolkien, Christopher Wiseman, Robert Gilson, and Geoffrey Bache Smith: the T.C.B.S., the Tea Club and Barrovian Society, the 'immortal four'. They believe themselves called to kindle a new light in the world through art and letters. This brotherhood is the first Fellowship of his life: a company of friends bound by love and high purpose. The war will shatter it, and out of that shattering the mythology will be born.
suggested_refs: site of Barrow's Stores, Corporation Street

segments.name: Oxford of the First Springtime, Exeter College and Éarendel

stops.name: Exeter College, Oxford, the undergraduate philologist
stops.campa: Tolkien comes up to Exeter College on an Open Classical Exhibition, but Classics cannot hold him. He steeps himself in Old English, Gothic, Welsh, and above all Finnish, the strange sweet tongue of the Kalevala, over which he pores until his examinations suffer. After a merely good Second in Honour Moderations he changes his school to English Language and Literature. In the Finnish grammar he finds the seed of a new invented language, high and vowel-rich, that he begins to build in his notebooks. He does not yet know that this Qenya will become the Latin of the Elves, the tongue of the Valinorean lords.
stops.quote: It was like discovering a complete wine-cellar filled with bottles of an amazing wine of a kind and flavour never tasted before. It quite intoxicated me.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on first reading Finnish, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: Cheltenham, the reunion at the railway station
stops.campa: On the very night of his twenty-first birthday, freed at last from his guardian's ban, Tolkien writes to Edith, now removed to Cheltenham, to say he loves her still and to ask her hand. She writes back that she is engaged to another. Within a week he takes the train to Cheltenham; she meets him on the platform. Before the day is out she returns her ring to the farmer and pledges herself instead to Ronald. The lovers, parted three years by an old priest's command, are joined again, and the pattern of Beren winning back Lúthien from a hopeless case is quietly, life-long, laid down.

stops.name: The Crist of Cynewulf: Éarendel, brightest of angels
stops.campa: Reading the Old English Crist of Cynewulf, Tolkien is stopped and shaken by a line: Eala Earendel engla beorhtast, ofer middangeard monnum sended, 'Hail Earendel, brightest of angels, above the middle-earth sent unto men.' A strange thrill runs through him, as if something long asleep had stirred. He feels behind the word a whole lost world he must recover. From this single line grows Earendil the Mariner, who sails his ship into the sky bearing a Silmaril as the morning star, and Middle-earth itself takes its name from that ancient poem's middangeard.
stops.quote: There was something very remote and strange and beautiful behind those words, if I could grasp it, far beyond ancient English.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on the Éarendel line, quoted in Carpenter, Biography
suggested_refs: manuscript of 'The Voyage of Éarendel the Evening Star'

stops.name: St Mary Immaculate, Warwick, the marriage
stops.campa: With the Somme gathering on the horizon and his commission already in hand, Tolkien marries Edith Bratt in the Catholic church of St Mary Immaculate at Warwick, beneath its castle. She has become a Catholic to marry him. They have a few weeks together before he must go. Warwick, with its castle and its old town, is for him already half-mythical, a town glimpsed as through a haze into a lost age; in his early poems it becomes Kortirion, the city of the fading Elves. Man and wife, they stand at the edge of the abyss into which his generation is about to fall.
suggested_refs: Church of St Mary Immaculate, Warwick

segments.name: The Fire of the Somme, the war that seeds the mythology

stops.name: Étaples, landfall in France
stops.campa: Second Lieutenant Tolkien of the 11th Battalion, Lancashire Fusiliers, disembarks at the vast base camp of Étaples and moves up toward the front as battalion signalling officer. He carries in his kit the beginnings of his invented languages and a growing sheaf of poems. Ahead lies the greatest battle Britain has yet fought. He is twenty-four. The mud, the wire, the dead men's world of the trenches, the loyal batmen at his side, the roar and desolation, all of it is going down now into the deep, to surface later as the Dead Marshes, as Mordor, as the servant Sam who never leaves his master.
stops.quote: Junior officers were being killed off, a dozen a minute. Parting from my wife then . . . it was like a death.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, foreword to The Lord of the Rings

stops.name: La Boisselle, the death of Rob Gilson
stops.campa: On the first morning of the battle, walking forward as if on parade, Robert Quilter Gilson of the T.C.B.S. is killed near La Boisselle. Word reaches Tolkien days later. Something in the great design of the four seems to crack; he writes to Smith that a member of the immortal band has fallen and asks whether their fellowship, their high dream, can survive. Grief and doubt wrestle in him. The war is beginning to take, one by one, the friends who first believed in his vocation, and to press him toward the tales that will keep faith with the dead.
stops.quote: My chief impression is that something has gone crack. I feel just the same to both of you — nearer if anything and very much in need of you . . . but I don't feel a member of a little complete body now.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien to G. B. Smith, August 1916, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: Ovillers and the Somme front, into the battle
stops.campa: In mid-July the battalion goes into the line before Ovillers, over ground already carpeted with the British dead of the first day. Tolkien lays and mends telephone wire under shellfire, sends runners and pigeons through the din, snatches sleep in dugouts. The 'animal horror' of trench warfare enters him. Here, amid the wreck of the immortal four, he grasps the truth his mythology will carry: that the small and overlooked, the private soldier, the plain hobbit, endure and matter more than the great. He survives assault after assault where thousands do not.
stops.quote: My 'Sam Gamgee' is indeed a reflexion of the English soldier, of the privates and batmen I knew in the 1914 war, and recognised as so far superior to myself.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 53
suggested_refs: Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme

stops.name: Beauval field hospital, struck down by trench fever
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of October, after four months in and out of the line, Tolkien falls sick with trench fever, the louse-borne illness that burns and racks him. Within a fortnight he is invalided back across the Channel to England. The fever that nearly kills him also saves him: it lifts him out of the meat-grinder that will devour so many who stay. Lying weak in the wards he begins, at last, to write down the great cycle of tales that has been forming in him: the mythology for England he had dreamed of with the T.C.B.S., now made urgent by the graves being dug behind him.

stops.name: Souastre, the death of G. B. Smith and the last charge to keep faith
stops.campa: Near Souastre, Geoffrey Bache Smith, the poet of the four, is struck by a shrapnel-burst as he walks along a road. Gangrene takes hold; on the third of December, at half past three in the morning, he dies. His last letter to Tolkien, written in expectation of death, lays a charge upon the survivor: that if he is scuppered, one of the great T.C.B.S. will still be left to say what they all dreamed. Of the immortal four, only Tolkien and Wiseman now remain. Tolkien edits and publishes Smith's poems, and takes up the dreamed work as a sacred trust: the mythology now a debt owed to the dead.
stops.quote: May you say the things I have tried to say long after I am not there to say them, if such be my lot. . . . Death can make us loathsome and helpless as individuals, but it cannot put an end to the immortal four!
stops.quote_source: G. B. Smith to Tolkien, 1916, quoted in Carpenter, Biography
suggested_refs: A Spring Harvest by G. B. Smith, edited by Tolkien

segments.name: The Book of Lost Tales, Convalescence and the Hemlock Glade

stops.name: Great Haywood, The Cottage of Lost Play begun
stops.campa: Convalescent at Great Haywood in Staffordshire, where Edith has come to be near him, Tolkien takes up a battered exercise-book and writes across it in his own invented script the title The Book of Lost Tales. On the twelfth of February he begins the first tale, The Cottage of Lost Play, in which the mariner Eriol comes over sea to the isle of the Elves and hears their histories. The great legendarium is born, not in a study but in a soldier's sick-leave, out of grief for the dead and love for the woman near him. The village where two rivers meet becomes, in the tales, the Elvish Tavrobel.
stops.quote: I have hardly written more than a chapter of the tale of Turambar . . . before some of the events have come true.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on the Lost Tales in wartime, Letters foreword
suggested_refs: The Book of Lost Tales manuscript notebooks

stops.name: Roos, in Holderness: Edith dances in the hemlock glade
stops.campa: Posted to command an outpost of the Humber Garrison, Tolkien walks with Edith in a small wood at Roos, thick with white hemlock in flower. There, in a sunlit glade, Edith dances for him and sings. In that moment the deepest of all his tales is conceived: a mortal man, Beren, comes upon Lúthien Tinúviel, fairest of the Children of Ilúvatar, dancing among the hemlocks, and loves her, and dares death and the Iron Crown to win her. He is Beren; she is Lúthien; the story is theirs. It becomes, he says, the kernel of the whole mythology, and the names will one day be cut upon their single grave.
stops.quote: In those days her hair was raven, her skin clear, her eyes brighter than you have seen them, and she could sing — and dance. . . . But the story has gone crooked, and I am left, and I cannot plead before the inexorable Mandos.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 340 (to Christopher Tolkien, 11 July 1972)
suggested_refs: hemlock glade at Roos, East Yorkshire

stops.name: Kingston upon Hull, the Fall of Gondolin written on army paper
stops.campa: Still weak with fever and posted about the Humber garrison, Tolkien writes on the backs of army marching-music the first and grandest of the tales: The Fall of Gondolin. The hidden Elven-city of seven names is betrayed and stormed by Morgoth's dragons and Balrogs of fire and iron; Tuor leads the survivors down the secret way while the towers burn. It is a battle-tale written by a man just out of the greatest battle of the age: the Somme's engines of steel transfigured into the foes of the Elves. That autumn his first son is born; the maker of worlds becomes a father in the ruin of the old.

segments.name: The Making of the Letters: Leeds, Oxford, and the Invented Scripts

stops.name: University of Leeds, the young professor and the runes
stops.campa: Tolkien takes a post as Reader, then Professor, of English Language at Leeds, the youngest on the staff. With his colleague E. V. Gordon he edits Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and drills students in Old and Middle English and the Norse sagas. Here his private mythology grows alongside his scholarship, and here he perfects the invented writing-systems that clothe his languages: the flowing Tengwar, whose shapes are built from the very features of the sounds they carry, and the angular Cirth, the runes cut for stone and wood. Like Barbier's night-writing and Braille's raised dots, his letters are a made script, a alphabet dreamed whole by one mind.
suggested_refs: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Tolkien & Gordon edition, 1925)

stops.name: The Tengwar and the Cirth, the sub-created alphabets
stops.campa: In the fictional deeps of his world the letters have their own history: the Tengwar are devised by Fëanor of the Noldor in Valinor, refining the older Sarati of Rúmil, their shapes a rational system where each stroke and bow marks a feature of speech. The Cirth, the runes, are made by the Grey-elves of Beleriand and elaborated by Daeron of Doriath into the Angerthas; the Dwarves take them up to carve in stone. He writes his diaries and book-titles in these hands, a maker of scripts as much as of stories, whose runes face the atlas's ciphers, the fingertip alphabets of the blind, the knotted quipu.
stops.quote: The Tengwar and the Certar (Runes) . . . were both of Elvish origin.
stops.quote_source: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E
suggested_refs: Tengwar title-page inscription of The Lord of the Rings

stops.name: Quenya and Sindarin, the two tongues and their kindred
stops.campa: In his notebooks the invented languages ripen into two great kindred tongues, each with its own music: Quenya, high and Latin-Finnish, the speech of the Elves of the Blessed Realm; and Sindarin, supple and Welsh, the tongue of the Grey-elves of Middle-earth. He works out their common ancestor, their sound-shifts, their divergence down the ages, as a philologist reconstructs Proto-Germanic behind English and Gothic. No man before has built a language so deep for love alone. And because a tongue must be written, he gives them the Tengwar and the Cirth, a whole civilisation of speech and script sub-created by one mind, to stand beside the world's true alphabets.
stops.quote: Nobody believes me when I say that my long book is an attempt to create a world in which a form of language agreeable to my personal aesthetic might seem real.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 205

stops.name: Pembroke College, Oxford: Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor
stops.campa: Elected Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon, Tolkien returns to Oxford with a fellowship at Pembroke College. For the next decades he lectures on Beowulf and the old poetry, opening his classes by declaiming its thunderous opening, Hwæt!, so that a hushed room hears the very voice of the ancestral North. His 1936 lecture on Beowulf, 'The Monsters and the Critics', changes forever how the poem is read, arguing that its dragon and its grief are the heart of the thing, not a flaw. In his study at Pembroke he will write, in the margins of his day-labour, both The Hobbit and the beginnings of the greater tale.
stops.quote: Hwæt! Wé Gárdena in géardagum, þéodcyninga þrym gefrúnon, hú ðá æþelingas ellen fremedon.
stops.quote_source: Beowulf, opening lines (Tolkien's lifelong text)

segments.name: In a Hole in the Ground, The Hobbit and the Inklings

stops.name: Magdalen College, the friendship with C. S. Lewis
stops.campa: At a meeting of the English faculty Tolkien first meets a stocky, argumentative young don from Magdalen, Clive Staples Lewis. They fall into deep talk, and one September night walking on Addison's Walk they argue until the small hours about myth: Tolkien holding that myths are not lies but broken lights of the true, and that in Christ the great myth had become fact. Lewis, an atheist, is moved toward belief. The two become the closest of friends and each other's chief encouragers; without Lewis's cheering-on, Tolkien later says, The Lord of the Rings would never have been finished.
stops.quote: The unpayable debt that I owe to him was not 'influence' as it is ordinarily understood, but sheer encouragement. He was for long my only audience.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 276
suggested_refs: photograph of Tolkien and C. S. Lewis

stops.name: 20 Northmoor Road, the blank page and the hobbit
stops.campa: One summer in his study at Northmoor Road, marking a great weary heap of School Certificate papers, Tolkien turns a page and finds one candidate has left a leaf blank. Onto that emptiness, without thought or plan, he writes: 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.' He does not know what a hobbit is, and so must find out. From that single unwilled sentence grows a story he tells his children by the fire: of Bilbo Baggins, the dragon Smaug, the ring found in the dark. And, unlooked-for, the door into all of Middle-earth swings open for the world to enter.
stops.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit. Not a nasty, dirty, wet hole, filled with the ends of worms and an oozy smell . . . it was a hobbit-hole, and that means comfort.
stops.quote_source: The Hobbit, opening lines
suggested_refs: Tolkien's map of Wilderland and Thror's Map

stops.name: The Hobbit published, the world enters Middle-earth
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of September, George Allen & Unwin of London publish The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, with the author's own maps and pictures. Stanley Unwin's small son Rayner, given the manuscript to judge for a shilling, has approved it. The book is an immediate success; the publisher, hungry for more, asks for a sequel about hobbits. Tolkien, hoping instead to give them his great mythology of the Silmarils, is turned back toward the little folk, and so, that winter, sits down to write what he thinks a short sequel, not knowing it will take him seventeen years and become The Lord of the Rings.
stops.quote: One writes such a story not out of the leaves of trees still to be observed . . . but it grows like a seed in the dark out of the leaf-mould of the mind.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 241

stops.name: University of St Andrews, the Andrew Lang lecture on Faërie
stops.campa: Before the University of St Andrews, Tolkien delivers the Andrew Lang lecture, 'On Fairy-Stories', and sets out the whole theology of his art. The teller of tales, he says, is a sub-creator, making a Secondary World the mind may enter and believe, an act that images the making of the great Creator whose child he is. And there is a good catastrophe, a eucatastrophe: the sudden joyous turn beyond hope that marks the true fairy-story. The Gospels hold the greatest of these: the Birth of Christ is the eucatastrophe of Man's history, the Resurrection its crown. His whole legendarium is here confessed as a work of faith.
stops.quote: The Birth of Christ is the eucatastrophe of Man's history. The Resurrection is the eucatastrophe of the story of the Incarnation. This story begins and ends in joy.
stops.quote_source: 'On Fairy-Stories', Epilogue
suggested_refs: 'On Fairy-Stories' in Essays Presented to Charles Williams (1947)

stops.name: The Eagle and Child, the Inklings in the Rabbit Room
stops.campa: On Tuesday mornings a company of friends gathers in the small back parlour of the Eagle and Child in St Giles': the pub they fondly call the Bird and Baby, the room the Rabbit Room. Here Lewis, Charles Williams, Hugo Dyson, Owen Barfield, Warnie Lewis and Tolkien drink beer, argue, and read aloud their works in progress. In this snug the world first hears, chapter by halting chapter, the tale of the Ring; here Narnia too is first spoken. The Inklings are the second and greatest Fellowship of his life: a company of makers, the T.C.B.S. reborn and, this time, surviving.
suggested_refs: The Eagle and Child, 49 St Giles', Oxford

segments.name: The Great Tale and the Long Defeat, The Lord of the Rings

stops.name: Merton College, the New Hobbit across seventeen years
stops.campa: Through the years of the Second War and after, in his study and among the Inklings, Tolkien labours at the sequel that keeps deepening and darkening until it is no children's tale but a vast heroic romance of a Ring of Power that must be unmade. In 1945 he is elected Merton Professor of English Language and Literature. The writing is slow, halting, abandoned and resumed across seventeen years; he despairs of it, revises endlessly, redraws his maps, works out the calendars and tongues behind every page. It is, he knows, the labour of his life: the great tale grown at last out of all the smaller ones.
stops.quote: I do not think that even Power or Domination is the real centre of my story. . . . The real theme for me is about something much more permanent and difficult: Death and Immortality.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 186
suggested_refs: Tolkien's manuscript drafts of The Lord of the Rings, Marquette University

stops.name: The Fellowship of the Ring published, the great tale comes forth
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of July, Allen & Unwin bring out The Fellowship of the Ring, first volume of The Lord of the Rings, with The Two Towers to follow in November and The Return of the King the next year. The publisher fears it will lose money; instead it slowly, then swiftly, conquers. Into it Tolkien has poured everything: the Shire that is Sarehole, the fallen friends who are Frodo's companions, the batmen who are Sam, the Marshes that are the Somme, the invented tongues and the runes, the long defeat lit by sudden grace. The mythology dreamed with the immortal four is given at last to the world.
stops.quote: I am in fact a Hobbit (in all but size). I like gardens, trees, and unmechanized farmlands . . . I like, and even dare to wear in these dull days, ornamental waistcoats.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 213
suggested_refs: first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring (1954)

stops.name: The Return of the King, the eucatastrophe and the Grey Havens
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October the third volume, The Return of the King, completes the tale, and with it the appendices: the calendars, the family trees, and the tables of the Tengwar and the Cirth laboured over for years. The Ring is unmade at the crack of doom by the failure of the very hobbit who bore it, and grace turns ruin to victory: the eucatastrophe he preached at St Andrews, made flesh. At the last, Frodo the wounded goes down to the Grey Havens and sails west over sea, into the light beyond the world's edge, healed of a hurt that will not heal on earth.
stops.quote: The grey rain-curtain turned all to silver glass and was rolled back, and he beheld white shores and beyond them a far green country under a swift sunrise.
stops.quote_source: The Return of the King, 'The Grey Havens'
suggested_refs: first edition of The Return of the King (1955)
Appendix E, the Tengwar and Cirth tables

segments.name: The Grey Havens: Bournemouth, Wolvercote, and the passing over sea

stops.name: Poole and the Hotel Miramar, the retreat from fame
stops.campa: Grown famous beyond bearing, besieged by admirers who telephone in the night and camp on his lawn, Tolkien takes Edith away to the mild seaside air of Poole, near Bournemouth, for her failing health. They live quietly in a bungalow; he keeps his study and his pipe and his invented alphabets; they holiday at the Hotel Miramar overlooking the sea. It is a kind of exile from Oxford, borne for love of her. The great work is done; the tales of the Elder Days he still cannot finish lie in their boxes. He waits, like his own Elves, at the shore of the world, near the end of an age.

stops.name: Wolvercote Cemetery, Edith as Lúthien upon the stone
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of November Edith dies at eighty-two. Tolkien, broken, returns to Oxford, to rooms Merton gives him. Upon her grave in the Catholic ground of Wolvercote he has cut, beneath her name, the single word Lúthien, for she was, and knew she was, his Lúthien, who danced for him among the hemlocks fifty years before. He writes to his son that he cannot now plead before the inexorable Mandos, lord of the dead, for the return of the one he loved; the story has gone crooked, and he is left behind, as Beren was left when Lúthien first died.
stops.quote: I never called Edith Lúthien — but she was the source of the story that in time became the chief part of the Silmarillion. . . . For she was (and knew she was) my Lúthien.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 340 (to Christopher Tolkien, 11 July 1972)
suggested_refs: grave of Edith and J.R.R. Tolkien, Wolvercote Cemetery

stops.name: Bournemouth, the passing of the maker
stops.campa: Visiting friends in Bournemouth, Tolkien is taken with a bleeding ulcer and then a chest infection, and on the second of September, one-and-twenty months after Edith, he dies at eighty-one. He is buried with her in the single grave at Wolvercote, and beneath his name is added the word Beren, so that the mortal man and the immortal maid lie together under the names of his own most beloved tale, made true at the last. He believed that beyond the circles of the world there was more than memory; that the fallen maker of secondary worlds might himself be a strand in the great Story still being told.
stops.quote: But all the stars are one to me; nor light of Sun nor moon I know, till on the hither shore once more I find the Haven long ago . . .
stops.quote_source: Tolkien, 'The Sea-Bell' (The Adventures of Tom Bombadil)
suggested_refs: Beren and Lúthien grave, Wolvercote Cemetery
posthumous first edition of The Silmarillion (1977)

stops.name: The Silmarillion, the great mythology given to the world
stops.campa: Four years after his father's death, Christopher Tolkien brings out at last The Silmarillion: the vast mythology of the Elder Days that Tolkien laboured over from the wards of the Great War until his death and never could finish. Here are the Music of the Ainur by which the world is sung into being, the theft of the Silmarils, the wars against Morgoth, and Beren and Lúthien at the centre, begun in a hemlock glade in 1917. The work dreamed with the immortal four, held as a debt to the dead across sixty years, comes forth complete. The maker has passed over sea, but the sub-creation stands.
stops.quote: There was Eru, the One, who in Arda is called Ilúvatar; and he made first the Ainur, the Holy Ones, that were the offspring of his thought.
stops.quote_source: The Silmarillion, 'Ainulindalë'
